nodes.name: Spike-rush & sedges
nodes.desc: Wetland sedge whose bulbs (corms) are eaten by magpie geese in the dry season. It grows in shallow water and mud on the floodplains.

nodes.name: Savanna grasses
nodes.desc: Tall grasses of the open woodland understorey. Fresh green shoots after a burn draw in wallabies and other grazers.

nodes.name: Darwin stringybark
nodes.desc: A dominant tree of the lowland eucalypt woodlands that cover most of the park. Its leaf litter and fallen wood feed the decomposers.

nodes.name: Paperbark
nodes.desc: A paperbark tree of wet lowlands and floodplain edges. Its flowers are visited by honeyeaters.

nodes.name: Floodplain algae
nodes.desc: Films of algae on plants and mud in billabongs and floodwater. They feed small fish and other aquatic grazers.

nodes.name: Magpie goose
nodes.desc: Floodplain bird that eats grass seeds, grass blades and spike-rush bulbs. It is the most recorded bird near the park and a seasonal food for people and crocodiles.

nodes.name: Agile wallaby
nodes.desc: Grazes mainly at night on grasses and herbs, often near rivers and billabongs. It is the most recorded mammal near the park and a staple prey of crocodiles and dingoes.

nodes.name: Feral water buffalo
nodes.desc: Introduced grazer that damaged floodplains and wetlands before most were removed. Carcasses feed kites and crows, and crocodiles also take buffalo.

nodes.name: Dusky rat
nodes.desc: Rodent of the cracking-clay floodplains, found in large numbers when the grass is lush. It is food for dingoes, kites and small carnivores.

nodes.name: Rainbowfish
nodes.desc: Small schooling fish of creeks and billabongs, part of the park's rich freshwater fish fauna. They graze algae and small insects and feed larger fish.

nodes.name: White-throated honeyeater
nodes.desc: Small bird of savanna woodland and paperbarks that feeds on nectar and insects.

nodes.name: Whistling kite
nodes.desc: Hunts small mammals, birds, fish and reptiles and eats carrion. It hovers at grass fires to catch fleeing prey.

nodes.name: Northern quoll
nodes.desc: Small carnivorous marsupial that eats invertebrates, small mammals, lizards and frogs. Cane toads have caused steep local declines in Kakadu.

nodes.name: Torresian crow
nodes.desc: Opportunistic scavenger and omnivore, often at carcasses.

nodes.name: Barramundi
nodes.desc: Predatory fish of estuaries and rivers that eats smaller fish, crustaceans and molluscs. Mangrove and tidal areas are used for breeding and feeding.

nodes.name: Freshwater crocodile
nodes.desc: Smaller crocodile of billabongs and creeks. It eats insects and fish, and ambushes larger prey like wallabies. Cane toads have hit its numbers hard.

nodes.name: Saltwater crocodile
nodes.desc: Apex ambush predator of rivers, floodplains and tidal flats. It takes magpie geese, wallabies, fish and large animals such as buffalo.

nodes.name: Dingo
nodes.desc: Top land predator that hunts wallabies, rodents, birds and young buffalo. Dingo predation is a major cause of quoll losses.

nodes.name: Monsoon floods
nodes.desc: Wet-season rain floods the plains for months, spreading nutrients and filling billabongs that support plants, fish and waterbirds.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Controlled burning with traditional owners shapes the savanna and flushes prey; too many fires have harmed some birds.

nodes.name: Tropical sun
nodes.desc: Year-round warmth and bright sun drive fast plant growth wherever there is water.

nodes.name: Floodplain soil
nodes.desc: Floodwaters deposit nutrients on the plains, building rich soils for sedges and grasses.

nodes.name: Termites, fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter, dead grass, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
